/-!
# Erdős Problem 248

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/248](https://www.erdosproblems.com/248)
- [TaTe25] T. Tao and J. Teräväinen, Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers. arXiv:2512.01739 (2025).
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.omega

namespace Erdos248

/--
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $\omega(n + k) \ll k$ for all $k \geq 1$?
Here $\omega(n)$ is the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos248.lean#L47"]
theorem erdos_248 : (∃ C > (0 : ℝ), { n | ∀ k ≥ 1, ω (n + k) ≤ C * k }.Infinite) := by
  sorry

end Erdos248

reformulations.difference: The source asks a yes/no question ('Are there infinitely many n such that, for all k≥1, ω(n+k) ≪ k?'). The Lean has no answer(...) slot: it asserts the affirmative directly. It spells out ≪ as one real constant C > 0 chosen before the infinitude claim, so C is uniform in n and k. It also lets n range over ℕ including 0, where the paper says positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) The problem was solved in the affirmative, and P is logically equivalent to `answer(True) ↔ P`. Sibling files such as erdos_69 use the same question-docstring / plain-assertion pattern. (2) Reading of ≪: erdosproblems.com and Tao–Teräväinen Theorem 1.1 both state the result as 'there exists an absolute constant C>0 such that for infinitely many (positive integers) n, for all (positive integers) k, ω(n+k) ≤ Ck'. A constant depending on n would make the question trivial, since ω(n+k) ≤ log₂(n+k) ≤ (log₂(n+1)+1)k for every k ≥ 1. So the uniform-C reading is the intended one. (3) I proved in Lean that the file's statement is equivalent to each of: (a) the version with n restricted to positive integers (dropping 0 removes at most one element and does not affect infinitude); (b) the version without the guard C > 0 (for C ≤ 0 the set is empty because ω(n+2) ≥ 1, and any C can be replaced by max C 1); (c) the version with the strict inequality ω(n+k) < Ck (take C+1, since k ≥ 1).

review.notes: The file has one declaration, Erdos248.erdos_248. Checked with pp.all: n and k are natural numbers, ω is ArithmeticFunction.cardDistinctFactors, and the inequality is compared in ℝ. ω is never evaluated at 0, because k ≥ 1. The statement is not trivially provable: it is the Tao–Teräväinen sieve theorem, and the linked Lean proof imports a large weighted-sieve development. Status is consistent with the source: the file says research solved with a formal_proof link; erdosproblems.com says 'PROVED (LEAN)'; the linked proof at L47 states the identical proposition, and its final assembly file contains no sorry. I did not check every imported file of that development. Style only, not a mathematical defect: the source is a yes/no question, and CONTRIBUTING prefers `answer(True) ↔ P` for a solved question; the file states P directly, as erdos_69 does. The file omits the site's further variants (Lau's ω(n+k) ≪ log k for k ≥ 2, and Ω in place of ω); that is an omission, not a misstatement. I did not read Erdős's original texts ([Er74b], a scanned PDF with no OCR available; [ErGr80, p.61], a book I could not access). Tao–Teräväinen cite both and state the conjecture in exactly the form the Lean uses.
